display_title: We carefully consider your suggestions and implement more experiments to reveal the effectiveness and make our conclusion more convincing.

content.title: We carefully consider your suggestions and implement more experiments to reveal the effectiveness and make our conclusion more convincing.
content.comment:
Thanks for the comments. Here is a summary for answering the concerns.

1. Taking the speech translation as an example, the basic model structure of this paper follows prior works. The main difference is the cross-model alignment loss used.

As we mentioned in related works, most recent cross-modal translation research works follow the cross-modal encoder -> semantic encoder -> semantic decoder framework. While our overall architecture also seems like prior works, our model has some significant differences from them. 

First, the adapter of our framework, which is a core part of such an end2end model, is designed with two trainable modules. To enable the end2end zero-shot alignment, the shared and trainable semantic encoder embedding plays as the semantic knowledge prior and the WRD distance plays as the learning signal for alignment. 

Second, the adaptor aims to deal with sequences in different lengths. The shrink mechanism doesn't require a fixed-length output which is often used in prior works (e.g., Chimera) for aligning with other embeddings, e.g., text embeddings. As for works that do not utilize the fixed-length representations, they have to adopt a "hard' loss for supervised training, e.g, MSE and mean pooling, which causes information deficiency. 

Third, our zero-shot module is essentially end2end compatible with supervised training, i.e. fine-tuning with end2end ST data, which enables us to compare our framework with not only end2nd zero-shot ST but also supervised ST.

Besides, for fair comparison with other zero-shot works, we didn't use pre-trained wav2vev2 as the acoustic encoder in many ST works (e.g., STEMM, Chimera). We hypothesize wav2vev2 may improve our performance.

2.  However, no experiments fairly show the advantage of the proposed loss compared to that in prior works. Simply copying results from prior papers is not a reasonable way.

Our proposed method mainly works well in zero-shot setting, and we already have ablation study on WRD loss in Table 2. The overall zero-shot loss has only two functions: CTC and WRD loss. Just sharing embedding without WRD loss makes our model reduce to a cascade model, because other parameters in the adapter cannot be trained. We also evaluate the gap between cascade and end2end model in zero-shot setting, and the results show our method can almost close the huge gap in previous works. 

In addition, suggested by Reviewer qpHn, [1] also explore the pseudo zero-shot setting in end2end ST. Their results almost close the gap but still indicates their cascade system is better than end2end model. We add the corresponding results in Table 2 of the revised version. 

[1] Tight Integrated End-to-End Training for Cascaded Speech Translation - https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.12167

|model|common|he|gap|ASR data|MT data|
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
|[1] cascade|25.9 |25.0 ||2300h|27M|
|[1] pseudo zero-shot|25.1|24.4|-0.7|2300h|27M|
|our cascade|25.21|25.32||1300h|4.5M|
|our pseudo zero-shot|26.52|25.46|+0.725|1300h|4.5M|

In above table, [1] extends our ASR and MT data into a much larger scale and achieve better cascade system than our cascade one. However, [1]'s cascade results are worse than our zero-shot end2end model with fewer data. This can also verify the effectiveness of our proposed zero-shot adaptor.

In supervised setting, while this is not the main contribution of our work, we would like to add a series ablation study results (Table 4 in Appendix of revised version) as followings,

|All models are finetuned from the zero-shot model with BLEU 24.00|BLEU|
|:---|:---|
|Zero-Shot then FT|29.22 (original Table 3)|
|Zero-Shot then FT w.o WRD loss| 28.86|
|Zero-Shot then FT w.o KD loss| 28.36|
|Zero-Shot then FT w.o CTC loss (need to freeze acoustic module)| 28.94|

The WRD loss is mainly helpful for zero-shot training and has less impact for the supervised training. Similar to previous ST works, we found that KD loss is more important. Because our shrinking adaptor depends on the CTC results, the CTC loss cannot be directly removed. So we freeze the pre-trained acoustic encoder including CTC layer. The results indicates the acoustic encoder is well-trained in zero-shot phrase, and the freezing has almost no impact when fine-tuning. We hope this helpful to investigate the effectiveness of our proposed loss function specifically.

Last but not least, for both zero-shot and supervised end2end ST experiments, we selected all the results reported by prior works and adopted for comparison with our work with an important principle, which is having the similar experiment settings, for example, the similar training/test data set and evaluation parameters (like beam size=5). The differences that may lead to unfairness would be emphasized in the caption of result tables. Hope this would explain the conviction of our comparison.

display_title: Thanks for the valuable comments. We mainly explain the difference between pseudo-labeling (using data augmentation) and pseudo zero-shot (using original data).

content.title: Thanks for the valuable comments. We mainly explain the difference between pseudo-labeling (using data augmentation) and pseudo zero-shot (using original data).
content.comment:
We will address your concerns in weaknesses.

1. This work should be compared with pseudo-labelling. I am not sure if the Pseudo Zero-Shot ST in table2 represents pseudo-labelling approach. Why don't people just use pseudo-labelling approach because of its simplicity?

Pseudo labelling [1] is a data augmentation method, and could be complementary strategy to our proposed method. It could be used for every end2end ST research work trained with external ASR data. Our pseudo zero-shot is an experimental setting rather than method, so the description is in experimental section 4.2. We will further explain it.

In regular zero-shot setting (shown as upper panel in Fig 2b of the revision), the ASR data (audio, transcription) and MT data (src, tgt) have no overlapping in source text. We train the model in two steps. The first step is to train regular NMT with MT data, including the semantic encoder and decoder. The second step is to train the cross-modal aligned ASR model with ASR data, including acoustic encoder, adaptor and semantic encoder(freezing). After the two-step training, the assembled model acoustic encoder->adaptor->semantic encoder/decoder becomes a zero-shot ST.

In pseudo zero-shot setting (shown as lower panel in Fig 2b of the revision), we assume a small scale supervised ST triplet data (audio, transcription, translation) is available. However, we don't directly use the (audio, translation) pairs in the end2end training. Instead, we split the supervised data into (audio, transcription) and (transcription, translation), and add them into ASR and MT datasets respectively. Then we follow the same two-step training in above zero-shot setting. We conduct this experiment because this scenario is closer to the real world. If using pseudo-labeling, we can obtain more MT data from ASR transcription and need to refine the NMT. We agree it will definitely improve zero-shot model, but this is out of our scope: the main purpose is to use the original data for the zero-shot learning. We add the discussion of [1] in related works. 

As suggested by Reviewer qpHn, [2] also explores our pseudo zero-shot setting. We add the corresponding results in the Table 2 of the revision.

|model|common|he|gap|ASR data|MT data|
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
|[1] cascade|25.9 |25.0 ||2300h|27M|
|[1] pseudo zero-shot|25.1|24.4|-0.7|2300h|27M|
|our cascade|25.21|25.32||1300h|4.5M|
|our pseudo zero-shot|26.52|25.46|+0.725|1300h|4.5M|

In summary, pseudo-labeling is an add-on data augmentation trick to construct more supervised data. Our method and pseudo labelling are two parallel methods that people can use both of them. 
 
[1] Leveraging weakly supervised data to improve end-to-end speech-to-text translation\
[2] Tight Integrated End-to-End Training for Cascaded Speech Translation 

2. Reusing the MT decoder for e2e ST is not a new thing, e.g., STEMM, contrastive-ST.

As we claimed in related works, most recent end2end ST works adopted the cross-modal encoder->semantic encoder->semantic decoder framework. Our model uses the similar overall architecture but has some significant differences.

First, the adapter, which is usually a core part of such an end2end model, is designed with two trainable modules. To enable the end2end zero-shot alignment, the shared and trainable semantic encoder embedding plays as the knowledge prior and the linear layer is learned by WRD distance as signal. 

Second, our adapter with the shrink mechanism doesn't require a fixed-length output which is often used in prior works like contrastive-ST (Chimera) for aligning with other embeddings. 

In addition, STEMM uses the external tool MFA to generate frame-level speech-transcription alignment as additional feature, which is essentially different from our approach. Besides, unlike other works, we didn't use pre-trained wav2vev2 as the acoustic encoder.

3. An ablation study is preferred.

In zero-shot setting, the zero-shot loss has two functions: CTC and WRD loss. Just sharing embedding without WRD loss makes our model reduce to a cascade model, because other parameters in the adapter cannot be trained. The results are in the original Table 2.

While the supervised model is not our main contribution, we would like to add the following ablation study (Table 4 in revision). 

Zero-Shot model: 24.00 (Table 3)\
Zero-Shot then FT: 29.22 (Table 3)\
Zero-Shot then FT w.o WRD loss: 28.86\
Zero-Shot then FT w.o KD loss: 28.36\
Zero-Shot then FT w.o CTC loss (frozen acoustic module): 28.94

The WRD loss is mainly helpful for zero-shot cross-modal alignment and has less impact for the supervised training. Similar to previous ST works, KD loss is more important. Because our shrinking adaptor depends on the CTC results, the CTC loss cannot be directly removed. So we freeze the acoustic encoder including CTC layer. The results shows the acoustic encoder is well-trained in zero-shot phrase, and the freezing has almost no impact.

We are excited to receive your nice appraisal. Actually, we spent a lot of time on zero-shot image translation experiments including data collection, which seems to be a rush part of our paper, to explore the effectiveness of our methods. However, due to a lack of proper end-to-end annotation data, it is difficult to explore the potential of supervised training in image translation. content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper discusses a mechanism to build end-to-end speech translation model from only ASR and MT data. They propose to match the textual representations with the representations from speech using the word rotators distance using just the transcription data and use that module towards training a machine translation model. The ASR system and the MT system can then be connected in an end-to-end trainable framework to build a speech translation system. The models fine-tuned end-to-end on the speech translation data present strong results matching or exceeding the cascaded systems.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths** - 
1) Leaving aside the novelty in cross-modal encoder (see weakness), the semantic encoder and decoder is very interesting. I like the approach towards using word rotator distance to match the speech and text embeddings. A big plus is that it matches embeddings of sequences with varying lengths.
2) The approach seems to be effective in terms of its results and the approach and the problem is well motivated.

**Weakness** - 
1) The paper is missing quite a bit of important citations, for example A.1 discusses that they use straight through estimators without providing any references for it [1]. Another and probably a more important one is [2], which also proposed a similar technique for shrinking speech representations using CTC Alignments. Similarly for Image to text translation, comparison with [3] would have been useful. 
2) There are many works that discuss other ways to combine ASR and MT data, for example compositional end-to-end speech translation models [4] and tightly integrated cascaded systems [5]. These models have had success in using the subtask data and used in IWSLT challenges [6,7].
3) I think comparing with CTC based cascaded systems is not a fair comparison as the CTC only performance without any language model or an attentional decoder can be quite bad. It is important to compare it with an ASR system that's trained using an attentional decoder. 
4) Section 3.2, I think the CTC best path during training is not the argmax but rather the viterbi path of all possible CTC alignments. Have you considered using that instead of the argmax during training? 
5) In order to show the effectiveness of the WRD loss, it would be good to show ablation which losses are important. I would be curious to know if just sharing the embeddings in cross-modal encoder and semantic encoder is enough. 

**Missing References** - 
1) Straight through estimators - https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.3432
2) CTC based compression - https://aclanthology.org/2021.eacl-main.57/
3) Image to text translation - https://aclanthology.org/2021.emnlp-main.576.pdf
4) Compositional E2E Speech Translation - https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.00573
5) Tight Integrated End-to-End Training for Cascaded Speech Translation - https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.12167
6) ESPnet-ST IWSLT 2021 Offline Speech Translation System - https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.00636
7) Without Further Ado: Direct and Simultaneous Speech Translation by AppTek in 2021 - https://aclanthology.org/2021.iwslt-1.5/

**Additional Questions** 
1) What is the reason behind the large improvement during fine-tuning? Is it the ASR WER that's improving? If you kept the semantic encoder and decoder frozen and only fine-tune the cross-modal encoder, how much improvement can you achieve? 
2) Since, there are so many loss functions involved, it would be good to provide ablations that present contributions from each.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper although is clear to read, is missing important citations which make the contributions seem larger than it might be. This also impacts the readability of the paper as the authors are focusing on explaining a lot of novelty instead of focusing on the main novel contribution of the paper. The work is reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: I like the approach of using WRD to match the speech and text representations. The results are convincing. Although some prior works that are directly related to this work are missing, including some of them which are presented as a novel contribution like the shrink mechanism. I believe this has also reduced the readability of this work and the authors could have used that space to do some interesting analysis and ablations that support their work.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Thanks for the insightful comments. Here is the response to additional questions for Reviewer qpHn.

content.title: Thanks for the insightful comments. Here is the response to additional questions for Reviewer qpHn.
content.comment:
We will address our main contribution first. As our paper title indicates, the main focus is the cross-modal translation in zero-shot setting, which means the ASR/OCR data and the MT data have no overlapped examples for transcription and source sentence. For example, the supervised data is particularly limited for image-text translation in real scenario. Most of experiments are also conducted on zero-shot setting, and the ASR/OCR data and MT data are even not in the same domain. The improvement over previous zero-shot ST methods for more than 10 BLEU points.

Additional Questions:
1. What is the reason behind the large improvement during fine-tuning? If only fine-tune the cross-modal encoder, how much improvement can achieve?

As we claimed in Sec 3, our zero-shot end2end ST model is compatible with supervised training. Once the supervised data is available, we can further fine-tune the zero-shot model. So the large improvement actually comes from the additional supervised ST data.

For the 2nd question, we conduct a new experiment in the 3rd phrase for supervised loss Eq.(8) by setting the parameters of the cross-modal encoder as trainable. In other words, the semantic encoder and decoder are frozen. On En-De v2, we have the following BLEU (Table 5 in Appendix of the revised version). 

|All models are finetuned from the zero-shot model with BLEU 24.00|BLEU|
|:---|:---|
|Zero-Shot then FT|29.22 (original Table 3)|
|Zero-Shot then FT by freezing semantic encoder/decoder|25.14|

The result becomes much worse. The main reason is that since the NMT teacher is frozen, the in-domain MT data from end-to-end supervised data is actually not used. So it's difficult for the ST decoder to adapt for the supervised data, i.e., the decoder is not a good language model.

2. There are so many loss functions involved, provide ablations that present contributions from each.

In zero-shot setting, we already have ablation study on WRD loss in Table 2. The overall zero-shot loss has two functions: CTC and WRD loss. Just sharing embedding without WRD loss makes our model reduce to a cascade model, because other parameters in the adapter cannot be trained. 

Since the supervised model is not the main discussed topic of this paper, we didn't explore the contribution of each loss in Eq (8). For response, we would like to do the ablation study on En-De v2 and have the following BLEU (Table 4 in Appendix of the revised version). 

|All models are finetuned from the zero-shot model with BLEU 24.00|BLEU|
|:---|:---|
|Zero-Shot then FT|29.22 (original Table 3)|
|Zero-Shot then FT w.o WRD loss| 28.86|
|Zero-Shot then FT w.o KD loss| 28.36|
|Zero-Shot then FT w.o CTC loss (need to freeze acoustic module)| 28.94|

The WRD loss is mainly helpful for zero-shot training and has less impact for the supervised training.
Similar to previous ST works, found that KD loss is more important. 
Because our shrinking adaptor depends on the CTC results, the CTC loss cannot be directly removed. So we freeze the pre-trained acoustic encoder including CTC layer. The results indicates the acoustic encoder is well-trained in zero-shot phrase, and the freezing has almost no impact when fine-tuning.

display_title: Thanks for the insightful comments. Here is the response to weaknesses for Reviewer qpHn.

content.title: Thanks for the insightful comments. Here is the response to weaknesses for Reviewer qpHn.
content.comment:
1. The paper is missing quite a bit of important citations, for example A.1 discusses that they use straight through estimators without providing any references for it [1]. Another and probably a more important one is [2], which also proposed a similar technique for shrinking speech representations using CTC Alignments. Similarly for Image to text translation, comparison with [3] would have been useful.

We add the references [1,2,3] accordingly in the revised version. The straight-through estimator is an optional method to construct the shrinking distribution and performs slightly worse. It is described in Appendix, so we didn't intend to overclaim the contribution on it. In the Page 4 of the submission, we have cited two earlier papers in 2019 and 2020 for CTC compression, and we add [2] as the third one. Different from [2], our shrinking adaptor is trainable and mainly used for cross-modal alignment, by leveraging the semantic embedding as prior knowledge and WRD distance as learning signal. For research work [3], we found this paper does not fall into the same scope as ours. It is a text translation work for robustness, and more like a (src)text-image-(tgt)text method. It uses the parallel translation text corpus and synthesizes text-line images from the source text. Then it builds an image to text translation model. It is not a zero-shot image2text translation, so it is difficult to compare with our experiment.

2. There are many works that discuss other ways to combine ASR and MT data, for example compositional end-to-end speech translation models [4] and tightly integrated cascaded systems [5]. These models have had success in using the subtask data and used in IWSLT challenges [6,7].

We add reference [4,5] accordingly in the revised version. Thanks for pointing out the compositional end-to-end ST model with two encoder-decoders. We think it could be possibly generalized to zero-shot ST. In [5], the authors conducted an experiment similar to our pseudo zero-shot ST on MuST-C En-De with 2300h ASR data and 27M MT data. We use only <1300h ASR data and <5M MT data. We add such results in the Table 2 of the revised version. Their performance on cascade model is better than ours due to more data. However, in end-to-end setting, ours performs even better than its cascade system. We think our zero-shot alignment adaptor is more powerful.

|model|common|he|gap|ASR data|MT data|
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
|[5] cascade|25.9 |25.0 ||2300h|27M|
|[5] pseudo zero-shot|25.1|24.4|-0.7|2300h|27M|
|our cascade|25.21|25.32||1300h|4.5M|
|our pseudo zero-shot|26.52|25.46|+0.725|1300h|4.5M|

3. I think comparing with CTC based cascaded systems is not a fair comparison as the CTC only performance without any language model or an attentional decoder can be quite bad. It is important to compare it with an ASR system that's trained using an attentional decoder.

We agree the reported cascade model is not the optimal. We've mentioned we use the plain CTC ASR model without any post-processing, like additional language model. For ablation purpose, we can observe improvement by zero-shot alignment adaptor when comparing with our reported cascade model. For this response, we observe above table. Even [5] uses 2x ASR data and 5x MT data, our zero-shot end2end ST performance is slightly better than [5]'s cascade system.

4. Section 3.2, I think the CTC best path during training is not the argmax but rather the viterbi path of all possible CTC alignments. Have you considered using that instead of the argmax during training?

We change the verbal from "best path" to "path via argmax". Because we have to do CTC inference during training, we prefer to use argmax for faster computation. And we think the alignment adaptor with WRD loss can correct minor errors. Use viterbi path is a good suggestion and future work.

5. In order to show the effectiveness of the WRD loss, it would be good to show ablation which losses are important. I would be curious to know if just sharing the embeddings in cross-modal encoder and semantic encoder is enough.

WRD loss has been discussed additional question 2.
